summary: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) finds link-layer addresses of neighbors. This document updates it to let routers proactively create a Neighbor Cache entry when a new IPv6 address is assigned, and recommends that nodes send unsolicited Neighbor Advertisements for new addresses. This reduces delay and packet loss when starting off-link connections.

eli5.summary: When you get a new address, you should announce it so the router already knows you. This document asks for that, so your first message does not wait.

questions: why does ipv6 router drop first packets
what is a stale neighbor cache entry
subtitle: Hosts announce new IPv6 addresses to routers so the first return packets do not get dropped.

tldr.problem: A router does not know a host's new global IPv6 address until return traffic arrives, so it starts address resolution then and, with only a tiny packet buffer, drops the extra packets.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts send unsolicited Neighbor Advertisements to the all-routers multicast address when they configure a new address, and routers create a STALE Neighbor Cache entry when they receive one for an unknown address.
tldr.outcome: Routers have a usable cache entry before the first return packet arrives, which cuts delay and packet loss for new off-link connections. The RFC updates RFC 4861.

today: RFC 9131 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2021 and it updates RFC 4861. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem With Silent New Addresses
sections.content:
Under RFC 4861, a router that receives a Neighbor Advertisement for an address it has no cache entry for SHOULD silently discard it. The reasoning is that the recipient has apparently not started any communication with the target. That works for on-link host-to-host traffic, but not for a host talking to off-link destinations.

After a host joins the network and gets a Router Advertisement, it can send traffic off-link straight away. The router has no entry for the host's global addresses. It only starts address resolution when the first return packet arrives, and routers keep only a small number of packets in the queue while waiting. Extra packets are likely to be dropped, which can cause visible packet loss and slowdowns.
sections.eli5: Imagine moving into a new house and sending letters, but the post office does not know your address yet. When replies arrive, they have to stop and look you up, and some get thrown away.

sections.title: How the Problem Plays Out
sections.content:
The typical case is a host that joins a network, forms a new address and uses it to reach the Internet. A common example is a mobile device sending probes to detect connectivity or a captive portal. Many implementations use Optimistic DAD so they can send those probes before duplicate address detection finishes.

When return traffic reaches the first-hop router, the router creates an INCOMPLETE entry and sends a Neighbor Solicitation to the solicited-node multicast address. It MUST buffer at least one data packet and MAY buffer more, but most routers buffer only a few and some just one. Later packets replace older ones in the buffer. If the host sent several probes in parallel, it may consider all but one of them failed.

The same thing happens with a new privacy address or after the router's Neighbor Cache has been flushed. The RFC notes that Happy Eyeballs can hide the problem in dual-stack networks, but it shows up clearly in IPv6-only environments, especially wireless ones.
sections.eli5: The router only learns who you are when the first reply comes back, and it can only hold one or two messages while it figures that out. If you sent a bunch at once, most are lost.

sections.title: What a Solution Needs
sections.content:
The RFC lists what a fix must do:

  • If the router has no entry, create a STALE entry before the first packet for that address arrives.
  • Work for Optimistic Addresses too, since those devices are the most affected.
  • Not override an existing entry if the address turns out to be a duplicate.
  • Update every first-hop router, because traffic can leave via one router and return via another.

It must also not make the problems in RFC 6583 worse and must stay compatible with that RFC's recommendations.
sections.eli5: A good fix has to tell every router in the building, work even for people who move in in a hurry, and never kick out the real owner of an address.

sections.title: The Two Changes
sections.content:
First, a node sends unsolicited Neighbor Advertisements (gratuitous NAs) when it assigns a new IPv6 address to an interface. They go to the all-routers multicast address ff02::2, so only routers are the target. With MLD snooping, switches then send them only to routers instead of flooding all nodes.

Second, a router that receives an unsolicited NA for an address with no cache entry creates one, in the STALE state. Behavior for an existing entry is unchanged. When return traffic arrives, the router can send a unicast Neighbor Solicitation instead of a multicast one.

The RFC argues this adds little multicast load. The extra traffic only matters if no return traffic arrives or the router does not create the entry, and it says the amount is a few orders of magnitude below the usual level of Neighbor Discovery multicast traffic.
sections.eli5: Step one: when you get a new address, shout it to the routers only. Step two: the router writes you down in its address book right away, marked as something to double-check later.

sections.title: Normative Text in RFC 4861 Terms
sections.content:
All normative text is in Section 6, which changes two places in RFC 4861. In Section 7.2.5, if no entry exists, hosts SHOULD silently discard the advertisement as before. Routers SHOULD create a new entry using the Target Link-Layer Address Option, and the entry state MUST be set to STALE. If the NA has no such option, the router SHOULD silently discard it.

In Section 7.2.6, a node that configures a new global IPv6 address SHOULD send up to MAX_NEIGHBOR_ADVERTISEMENT Neighbor Advertisements. For a preferred address the Override flag SHOULD NOT be set. For an Optimistic Address it MUST NOT be set. The destination SHOULD be the all-routers multicast address, and the messages MUST be separated by at least RetransTimer seconds.

The first advertisement goes out as soon as a new Optimistic Address is assigned (if Optimistic DAD is used) or as soon as an address changes from tentative to preferred (if not).
sections.eli5: The rules say: routers should add new neighbors to their list, and newcomers should announce themselves a few times without pushing anyone else out of the list.

sections.title: Duplicate Addresses and Security
sections.content:
Section 5 walks through what happens if a host announces an Optimistic Address that someone else rightfully owns. Because the Override flag is clear, an existing cache entry is not updated with the new link-layer address. The risky cases need two hosts to act almost simultaneously, within tens of milliseconds in most cases. In the worst case the owner's traffic can be disrupted for about 7 seconds, which the RFC computes from the RFC 4861 constants and judges acceptable because the scenario is unlikely. A rightful owner that also sends unsolicited NAs avoids the disruption altogether.

The Security Considerations section adds that the change creates no new way to override an existing entry. A malicious host could try to fill a router's cache with STALE entries, but could already do so with a Neighbor Solicitation or Router Solicitation carrying a source link-layer address option, and the RFC 6583 advice still applies. Announcing to the all-routers address can reveal addresses to an on-link attacker, but DAD already discloses them to all nodes if MLD snooping is off.
sections.eli5: If two kids claim the same name, the teacher keeps the original entry. The worst case is a few seconds of confusion, and the real owner can prevent even that by announcing first.

sections.title: Limits and Alternatives Considered
sections.content:
The solution does not remove every case. A host that reuses an old address after a long quiet period may find the router has already deleted its entry, and clearing a router's Neighbor Cache still causes loss for active addresses.

The RFC also lists discarded alternatives: doing nothing, moving to registration-based Neighbor Discovery (RFC 8505), having the host send a Neighbor Solicitation or Router Solicitation from its global address, gleaning from DAD messages, sending data packets to the router, making host probing more robust, enlarging router buffers, and having routers resolve source addresses of transit traffic. Each is rejected for reasons such as not working with Optimistic Addresses, reaching only one of several routers, extra router load, or making cache exhaustion attacks easier.
sections.eli5: It is not perfect: if you go quiet for a long time you may be forgotten. The authors also looked at other ideas and found each had its own problem.
